1. Two point charges are placed in vacuum. A positive charge +𝑞 is located at the origin, and
a negative charge −𝑞 is located at a position on the positive 𝑥-axis. What is the direction of
the Coulomb force acting on −𝑞 , and what is the direction of the unit vector used in the
Coulomb force equation for that force?
A. Force on −𝑞 points in the +𝑥 direction; unit vector points in the +𝑥 direction
B. Force on −𝑞 points in the −𝑥 direction; unit vector points in the −𝑥 direction
C. Force on −𝑞 points in the −𝑥 direction; unit vector points in the +𝑥 direction
D. Force on −𝑞 points in the +𝑥 direction; unit vector points in the −𝑥 direction
questions.stem: Two point charges are placed in vacuum. A positive charge +𝑞 is located at the origin, and a negative charge −𝑞 is located at a position on the positive 𝑥-axis. What is the direction of the Coulomb force acting on −𝑞 , and what is the direction of the unit vector used in the Coulomb force equation for that force?

options.text: Force on −𝑞 points in the +𝑥 direction; unit vector points in the +𝑥 direction
options.explanation: This incorrectly treats the attractive force as if it pointed away from +q. It also ignores that with opposite charges the force is opposite the chosen separation unit vector.

options.text: Force on −𝑞 points in the −𝑥 direction; unit vector points in the −𝑥 direction
options.explanation:
The force direction is correct (attraction toward the origin), but the usual 
unit vector \(\hat{\mathbf r}\) in Coulomb’s law is taken from the source charge (+q) to the field point (−q), i.e. +x here. This option uses the opposite convention for the unit vector.

options.text: Force on −𝑞 points in the −𝑥 direction; unit vector points in the +𝑥 direction
options.explanation: The force on −q is attractive toward +q at the origin, so it points in the \(−x\) direction. Using \(\mathbf F = k\,q_1 q_2\,\hat{\mathbf r}/r^2\) with \(\hat{\mathbf r}\) pointing from +q (origin) to −q (on +x) gives \(\hat{\mathbf r}\) in +x, and since \(q_1 q_2<0\), the force is opposite \(\hat{\mathbf r}\), i.e. −x.

options.text: Force on −𝑞 points in the +𝑥 direction; unit vector points in the −𝑥 direction
options.explanation: This reverses the attractive force direction; −q should be pulled toward the origin (−x). It also mismatches the separation unit vector direction relative to the standard source-to-field-point definition.

questions.stem: A positive point charge +𝑄 is fixed at the origin. A negative point charge −𝑄 is placed on the positive 𝑦-axis. Which statement correctly describes the direction of the electric field at that point and the direction of the electric force on this negative charge?

options.text: Electric field upward; electric force upward
options.explanation: The electric field due to +Q is upward at +y, but a negative charge experiences force opposite \(\mathbf E\). This choice forgets \(\mathbf F = q\mathbf E\) reverses direction for \(q<0\).

options.text: Electric field upward; electric force downward
options.explanation: At a point on the +y-axis, the electric field from a positive charge at the origin points away from the origin (upward, +y). The force on the charge is \(\mathbf F = q\mathbf E\); since \(q=-Q\), the force is opposite the field (downward, −y).

options.text: Electric field downward; electric force upward
options.explanation: This reverses the direction of \(\mathbf E\): the field from +Q points away from the origin, not toward it. It also incorrectly pairs the force direction with that reversed field.

options.text: Electric field downward; electric force downward
options.explanation: The field direction is wrong: \(\mathbf E\) at +y from +Q points upward. With the correct \(\mathbf E\), the force on a negative charge would be downward, not matching both parts here.

3. A point charge is located at the center of a cube that acts as a Gaussian surface. Which
statement is correct?
A. Electric flux is zero through each face
B. Electric flux is the same through each face
C. The magnitude of electric field is the same everywhere on each face
D. None of the above is correct.
questions.stem: A point charge is located at the center of a cube that acts as a Gaussian surface. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Electric flux is zero through each face
options.explanation: The net flux through the entire closed surface is \(\Phi=Q_{enc}/\varepsilon_0\neq 0\) for a nonzero enclosed charge. Therefore the flux through each face cannot be zero.

options.text: Electric flux is the same through each face
options.explanation: By symmetry, the cube’s six faces are equivalent when the charge is at the center. Since the total flux is \(\Phi_{tot}=Q_{enc}/\varepsilon_0\), each face must carry \(\Phi_{face}=\Phi_{tot}/6=Q_{enc}/(6\varepsilon_0)\).

options.text: The magnitude of electric field is the same everywhere on each face
options.explanation: While the flux can be equal by symmetry, \(|\mathbf E|\) varies across a face because points on the face are at different distances from the central charge. This confuses constant flux with uniform field magnitude.

options.text: None of the above is correct.
options.explanation: Option B is correct by symmetry and Gauss’s law, so “none of the above” is incorrect. The mistake is overlooking that equal flux per face does not require uniform \(|\mathbf E|\) on a face.

cylindrical Gaussian surface is coaxial with the line charge. Which part(s) of the surface have
nonzero electric flux?
A. Only the curved side surface
B. Only the two flat circular end caps
C. Both the curved surface and the end caps
D. No part of the surface
questions.stem: An infinitely long straight line carries a uniform positive linear charge density. A closed cylindrical Gaussian surface is coaxial with the line charge. Which part(s) of the surface have nonzero electric flux?

options.explanation: For an infinite line charge, \(\mathbf E\) is radial and perpendicular to the curved side of a coaxial cylinder, so \(\mathbf E\cdot d\mathbf A\neq 0\) there. On the flat end caps, \(d\mathbf A\) points along the cylinder axis while \(\mathbf E\) is radial (parallel to the caps), giving \(\mathbf E\cdot d\mathbf A=0\) on the caps.

options.text: Only the two flat circular end caps
options.explanation: This assumes field lines pass through the caps, but for a line charge the field is radial, not axial. Thus the flux through end caps is zero.

options.text: Both the curved surface and the end caps
options.explanation: The end caps have zero flux because \(\mathbf E\) is parallel to their surfaces, making \(\mathbf E\cdot d\mathbf A=0\). Only the curved surface contributes.
A Gaussian cylinder encloses charge, so the total flux must be \(Q_{enc}/\varepsilon_0\neq 0\). The nonzero flux comes from the curved side surface.

5. A positive point charge +𝑞 and a negative point charge −𝑞 are separated by a distance 𝑟 in
vacuum. The distance between the two charges is then increased to 2𝑟. How does the electric
potential energy of the two-charge system change?
A. It increases (i.e., becomes more positive or less negative)
B. It decreases (i.e., becomes less positive or more negative)
C. It becomes zero.
D. It remains unchanged (but not zero).
questions.stem: A positive point charge +𝑞 and a negative point charge −𝑞 are separated by a distance 𝑟 in vacuum. The distance between the two charges is then increased to 2𝑟. How does the electric potential energy of the two-charge system change?

options.text: It increases (i.e., becomes more positive or less negative)
options.explanation: The potential energy of two point charges is \(U = k\,q_1 q_2 / r\). Here \(q_1 q_2 = -q^2\), so \(U(r)=-kq^2/r\) and \(U(2r)=-kq^2/(2r)\), which is less negative than before, i.e. the energy increases.

options.text: It decreases (i.e., becomes less positive or more negative)
options.explanation: This would be true for like charges (positive \(U\)), but for opposite charges \(U\) is negative and becomes less negative as separation increases. The misconception is treating the sign like the magnitude only.
For finite separation, \(U = -kq^2/r\neq 0\). It only approaches 0 as \(r\to\infty\).
Since \(U\propto 1/r\), changing the separation changes the potential energy. The error is assuming potential energy depends only on charges, not distance.

6. A charged particle moves from point A to point B in a uniform electric field. Which factor
determines the electric potential difference between A and B?
A. The path taken between A and B
B. The speed of the particle
C. The displacement component along the electric field
D. The mass of the particle
questions.stem: A charged particle moves from point A to point B in a uniform electric field. Which factor determines the electric potential difference between A and B?

options.text: The path taken between A and B
options.explanation: In electrostatics the field is conservative, so \(\Delta V\) is path-independent. This confuses electric potential difference with nonconservative work (like friction).
\(\Delta V\) depends on positions in the field, not on how fast the particle moves. The misconception is mixing up kinetic effects with potential difference.

options.text: The displacement component along the electric field
options.explanation: For a uniform field, \(\Delta V = -\int_A^B \mathbf E\cdot d\mathbf l = -\mathbf E\cdot\Delta\mathbf r\). Thus only the component of displacement along \(\mathbf E\) affects the potential difference; perpendicular motion contributes zero to \(\mathbf E\cdot d\mathbf l\).
Electric potential difference is a property of the field and geometry, not of the particle’s mass. This confuses gravitational potential ideas with electric potential.

doubled while the plate area remains unchanged, the capacitance:
A. Doubles
B. Is unchanged

questions.stem: A parallel-plate capacitor has plate area 𝐴 and plate separation 𝑑. If the plate separation is doubled while the plate area remains unchanged, the capacitance:

options.explanation: Capacitance does not increase with separation; it decreases. This mistake comes from thinking “more space stores more charge,” ignoring the field/voltage relation.
For parallel plates \(C\) depends on geometry via \(C=\varepsilon_0 A/d\). Doubling \(d\) must change \(C\).

options.text: Is reduced by a factor of 2
options.explanation: For a parallel-plate capacitor (vacuum), \(C=\varepsilon_0 A/d\). If \(d\to 2d\) with the same \(A\), then \(C\to \varepsilon_0 A/(2d)=C/2\), i.e. reduced by a factor of 2.

options.text: Is reduced by a factor of 4
options.explanation: A factor of 4 reduction would occur if separation were quadrupled, not doubled. The misconception is applying a square dependence (like inverse-square laws) to capacitance.

charges? (𝑘 = 8.99×109𝑁∙m2⁄𝐶2)
A. 28.8×106𝑁/𝐶
B. 14.4×106𝑁/𝐶
C. 7.19×106𝑁/𝐶
D. 0
questions.stem: Two point charges are separated by 10.0 cm and have charges of +2.00𝜇𝐶 and −2.00𝜇𝐶, respectively. What is the magnitude of the electric field at a point midway between the two charges? (𝑘 = 8.99×109𝑁∙m2⁄𝐶2)

options.explanation: This effectively double-counts again (e.g., using an incorrect distance) and overestimates the field. The common error is not using the midpoint distance \(r=0.05\,\text{m}\) from each charge correctly.

At the midpoint, each charge is \(r=0.05\,\text{m}\) away, so each contributes \(E_1=k|q|/r^2\). The fields point in the same direction (away from + and toward −), so magnitudes add: \(E=2k|q|/r^2 = 2(8.99\times10^9)(2.00\times10^{-6})/(0.05)^2 \approx 1.44\times10^7\,\text{N/C}=14.4\times10^6\,\text{N/C}.\)
This equals the field from only one charge at the midpoint, but the second charge’s field does not cancel here. The misconception is thinking opposite charges always cancel the field at the midpoint.

At the midpoint between equal and opposite charges, the fields point the same way (from + toward −), so they add rather than cancel. Zero field would occur at the midpoint for equal like charges, not opposite charges.

questions.stem: A total charge of −6.50𝜇𝐶 is uniformly distributed within an insulating sphere that has a radius of 0.150𝑚. What is the magnitude and direction of the electric field at 0.300𝑚 from the surface of the sphere?

options.explanation: The point is outside the sphere: distance from center \(r=0.150+0.300=0.450\,\text{m}\). By Gauss’s law, the external field equals that of a point charge: \(E=k|Q|/r^2=(8.99\times10^9)(6.50\times10^{-6})/(0.45)^2\approx2.89\times10^5\,\text{N/C}\); because the charge is negative, the field points radially inward.
The direction is wrong for a negative total charge (field should point inward). The magnitude is also too large, likely from using the wrong distance from the center.

While the inward direction matches a negative charge, the magnitude is incorrect because the correct radius is \(0.45\,\text{m}\) and \(E\propto 1/r^2\). This reflects using an incorrect \(r\) in \(E=k|Q|/r^2\).

options.text: None of the above is correct
options.explanation: Using Gauss’s law gives \(E\approx2.89\times10^5\,\text{N/C}\) inward, which matches option A. The mistake is overlooking that outside a uniformly charged sphere the field is identical to a point charge at the center.

questions.stem: A particle with charge +𝑄 is placed in the center of an initially uncharged conducting hollow sphere. What are the charges induced on the inner and outer surfaces of the sphere?

options.explanation: In electrostatic equilibrium, the electric field inside the conductor must be zero, so a charge \(−Q\) is induced on the inner surface to cancel the field from the central +Q within the metal. Because the conductor was initially neutral, the remaining +Q must appear on the outer surface so that total induced charge sums to zero.
If −Q appears on the inner surface, conservation of charge requires +Q somewhere else on the conductor. The misconception is forgetting the conductor’s net charge must remain zero.
A central charge in a conducting cavity must induce charge on the inner surface to keep \(\mathbf E=0\) within the conductor. This ignores the electrostatic shielding condition in the metal.

The inner surface cannot remain uncharged because the conductor must cancel the field within the metal. Also, a neutral conductor cannot end with net −Q on its outer surface without acquiring extra charge from elsewhere.

options.explanation: The electric field is the negative gradient of potential: \(\mathbf E = -\nabla V\). In 1D, \(E_x = -dV/dx = -(-15x+3)=15x-3\), so \(\mathbf E=(15x-3)\hat{\mathbf i}\).
This equals \(dV/dx\), not \(-dV/dx\). The misconception is missing the minus sign in \(\mathbf E=-\nabla V\).
This results from incorrectly integrating or differentiating as if \(V\) were cubic/quartic in \(x\). The error is applying the wrong power rule to \(V=-7.5x^2+3x\).
This is another incorrect power-rule result unrelated to \(-dV/dx\) for the given quadratic potential. The misconception is treating \(V\) as if it contained higher powers of \(x\).

12. A 10𝑉 battery is connected in series with a 2𝜇𝐹 capacitor, a 2Ω resistor, an ammeter, and a
switch that is initially open. A voltmeter is connected in parallel across the capacitor. At the
instant the switch is closed, what are the ammeter and voltmeter readings, respectively?
A. 0A, 10V
B. 0A, 0V
C. 5A, 0V
D. 5A, 10V
questions.stem: A 10𝑉 battery is connected in series with a 2𝜇𝐹 capacitor, a 2Ω resistor, an ammeter, and a switch that is initially open. A voltmeter is connected in parallel across the capacitor. At the instant the switch is closed, what are the ammeter and voltmeter readings, respectively?

options.explanation: At \(t=0^+\), an uncharged capacitor behaves like a short, so current is not zero. The 10 V initially appears across the resistor, not across the capacitor.
The capacitor voltage is indeed 0 V at \(t=0^+\), but the current is \(I(0^+)=V/R\neq 0\). The misconception is thinking a capacitor always blocks DC instantly.

Immediately after closing the switch, the capacitor is uncharged so \(V_C(0^+)=0\) and it behaves like a short circuit. Thus the full battery voltage is across the resistor and \(I(0^+)=V/R=10\,\text{V}/2\,\Omega=5\,\text{A}\), while the voltmeter across the capacitor reads 0 V.

If the capacitor had 10 V across it at that instant, the resistor would have 0 V and the current would be 0 A. The mistake is mixing up the initial (uncharged) and long-time (fully charged) capacitor behavior.

13. A 6.5𝑉 battery with negligible internal resistance is used to charge a 1.8𝑚𝐹 capacitor
through a 320Ω resistor. What is the time required for the capacitor charge to reach 44% of
its maximum value?
A. 0.47 s
B. 0.33 𝑠
C. 1.0 𝑠
D. 1.4 𝑠
questions.stem: A 6.5𝑉 battery with negligible internal resistance is used to charge a 1.8𝑚𝐹 capacitor through a 320Ω resistor. What is the time required for the capacitor charge to reach 44% of its maximum value?

options.explanation: Using \(q/Q_{\max}=1-e^{-t/RC}\), 44% corresponds to \(t=-RC\ln(0.56)\approx0.334\,\text{s}\), not 0.47 s. The likely error is using the wrong logarithm value or fraction.

For RC charging, \(q(t)=Q_{\max}(1-e^{-t/RC})\). Setting \(q/Q_{\max}=0.44\) gives \(e^{-t/RC}=0.56\) so \(t=-RC\ln(0.56)\); with \(R=320\,\Omega\) and \(C=1.8\,\text{mF}\), \(RC=0.576\,\text{s}\) and \(t\approx0.334\,\text{s}\approx0.33\,\text{s}.\)

This is much larger than the time constant \(RC=0.576\,\text{s}\); reaching 44% happens in less than one time constant. The misconception is thinking it takes about one \(RC\) to reach any substantial fraction.
1.4 s is about 2.4 time constants, which would correspond to a much larger fraction of full charge (near 91%). The error is misapplying the exponential charging curve.

of its velocity being 𝑣 = 5.0×105𝑚/𝑠 and 𝑣 = 3.0×105𝑚/𝑠. A magnetic field of 0.80 T
is in the positive y direction. At that instant, the magnetic force on the electron is:
A. (3.8×10−14𝑁)𝑘̂
B. (−6.4×10−14𝑁)𝑘̂

questions.stem: At one instant an electron (𝑞 = −1.6×10−19𝐶) is moving in the xy plane, the components of its velocity being 𝑣 = 5.0×105𝑚/𝑠 and 𝑣 = 3.0×105𝑚/𝑠. A magnetic field of 0.80 T is in the positive y direction. At that instant, the magnetic force on the electron is:

options.explanation: The magnitude does not match \(|q|v_xB\) (which gives \(6.4\times10^{-14}\,\text{N}\)). The likely error is using the wrong velocity component or arithmetic.

Magnetic force is \(\mathbf F=q\,\mathbf v\times\mathbf B\). With \(\mathbf B = B\hat{\mathbf j}\) and \(\mathbf v=v_x\hat{\mathbf i}+v_y\hat{\mathbf j}\), \(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B = v_xB\,\hat{\mathbf k}\); multiplying by electron charge \(q<0\) gives direction \(−\hat{\mathbf k}\). Magnitude is \(|F|=|q|v_xB=(1.6\times10^{-19})(5.0\times10^{5})(0.80)=6.4\times10^{-14}\,\text{N}.\)

This has the correct magnitude but the wrong sign; it corresponds to a positive charge. The misconception is forgetting the electron’s charge is negative, reversing the direction of \(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B\).

The direction (−\(\hat{\mathbf k}\)) could be plausible for an electron, but the magnitude is incorrect (should be \(6.4\times10^{-14}\,\text{N}\)). The error is using the wrong velocity component or miscalculating \(|q|vB\).
